content:
Christians say the New Testament speaks with one voice on salvation. On the central question, how a person is made right with God, two of its letters answer in words that face each other. Paul writes: "We maintain therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law" (Romans 3:28). James writes: "You see then that by works, a man is justified, and not only by faith" (James 2:24).[1]

Both use the same word, "justified". Both cite the same verse about Abraham. The Reformation turned on the difference.

This article aims to provide context to the tension, insha'Allah, in six points from the two letters, with the Christian reconciliation stated fairly. The Quran joins the two things the letters pull apart: "Except such as have Faith, and do righteous deeds" (103:3).[2]

Paul: "justified by faith apart from the works of the law" (Romans 3:28). James: "by works, a man is justified, and not only by faith" (James 2:24).[1]

Christian scholars answer that the two writers fight different errors. Felix Just, a Jesuit scholar of the New Testament, sums up the usual reconciliation: "There are differences in emphasis, but no contradictions in teaching, if one understands both properly." He suggests that James "intended to correct some misinterpretations of Paul's teachings."[3] If James is correcting readers of Paul, the readers were reading Paul's words, and the correction is aimed at what those words had been taken to mean.

Paul and James both quote Genesis 15:6: "Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness" (Romans 4:3).[1] Paul argues from its timing: Abraham was counted righteous "not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision" (Romans 4:10), before the sign was given in Genesis 17.

James argues from a later event, the binding of Isaac in Genesis 22: "Wasn't Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar? You see that faith worked with his works, and by works faith was perfected" (James 2:21 to 22).[1] One proof is a belief before any deed, and the other is a deed that completes the belief.

The Quran tells the same sacrifice, and joins faith to deed in one sentence: "So when they had both submitted their wills (to Allah) ... We called out to him 'O Abraham! Thou hast already fulfilled the vision!'" (37:103 to 105).[2] It calls Abraham "a model, devoutly obedient to Allah, (and) true in Faith" (16:120).

Christian scholars point out that Paul's "works of the law" are the rules of the Torah, above all circumcision, while James's "works" are good deeds.[3] James's example is plain: "if a brother or sister is naked and in lack of daily food, and one of you tells them, 'Go in peace, be warmed and filled'; and yet you didn't give them the things the body needs, what good is it?" (James 2:15 to 16).[1]

The distinction helps, and it does not cover everything Paul says. In Romans 4 he sets faith against work of any kind: "Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed. But to him who doesn't work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness" (Romans 4:4 to 5).[1] That sentence is about wages and labour, and circumcision is not in it.

"You believe that God is one. You do well. The demons also believe, and shudder" (James 2:19).[1] James's point is that agreeing with a true statement makes no one righteous; the demons know who God is and remain demons.

Paul did not teach a faith without conduct. He lists "the deeds of the flesh" and warns "that those who practice such things will not inherit God's Kingdom", and he names "faith working through love" as what counts (Galatians 5:6, 19 to 21).[1] The difference lies in what he says the conduct is for. In Paul it follows justification; in James it is part of it.

The churches have never settled the matter in one way. Protestant churches teach justification by faith alone, and hold that true faith produces good works. The Catholic Church teaches that a person cannot earn the first grace of justification, and places more weight on the believer's transformation and cooperation with grace. Eastern Orthodox teaching frames salvation as healing and participation in God, outside the terms of the Western debate.

All of them teach that conduct matters. They differ over its place, and the argument began with two letters in the same canon. Apostle of Doom traces the Pauline doctrine to its sources in justification and the Logos, and James's standing in James, the brother of ʿĪsā.

The Quran never sets faith against deeds. "If any do deeds of righteousness,- be they male or female - and have faith, they will enter Heaven, and not the least injustice will be done to them" (4:124).[2] Surah al-ʿAsr puts all mankind "in loss, Except such as have Faith, and do righteous deeds, and (join together) in the mutual teaching of Truth, and of Patience and Constancy" (103:2 to 3).[2]

It also denies that deeds buy Paradise. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Do good deeds properly, sincerely and moderately, and receive good news because one's good deeds will not make him enter Paradise." Asked, "Even you, O Allah's Messenger?", he answered: "Even I, unless and until Allah bestows His pardon and Mercy on me."[4] Faith and deeds are both required, and salvation rests on God's mercy, with no sacrifice of another standing in between.

The bottom line

Paul says a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law, and James says a man is justified by works and not by faith only. Both cite Abraham's faith in Genesis 15:6, Paul from before his circumcision and James from the sacrifice of his son. Christian scholars reconcile them by reading the two kinds of works differently, but Paul's own words in Romans 4 reach beyond the Torah, and the churches still divide over the question.

The Quran has no such tension to resolve. It names faith and righteous deeds together in verse after verse, and places salvation in God's mercy. Abraham, in its account, "fulfilled the vision" (37:105): his faith and his obedience were one act.[2] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Romans 3:28; 4:3 to 5; 4:10; James 2:15 to 24; Galatians 5:6, 19 to 21 (World English Bible).
  2. Quran 4:124; 16:120; 37:103 to 105; 103:1 to 3, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Felix Just, S.J., "Paul & James on Faith & Works", Catholic Resources (catholic-resources.org).
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Softening of the Hearts (al-Riqaq), the report of Aisha on deeds and mercy.
